Decision Models as Judges for Hallucination Detection

Haozheng Liu ††thanks: Corresponding authors: Haozheng Liu and Lingyao Li.
   Emails: hl6602@nyu.edu, lingyaoli@arizona.edu. Affiliation: New York University    Zhaoqian Xue Affiliation: University of Arizona    Zhongyin Wang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Junting Mu Affiliation: University of California, Irvine    Zihui Ma Affiliation: Emory University Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park    Shuya Feng Affiliation: University of Alabama at Birmingham    Lingyao Li22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: University of Arizona
Abstract

Large language models are widely used as judges of model outputs (LLM-as-a-Judge), but they are costly and can hallucinate or be overconfident. Decision models are a potential alternative. They return a predefined verdict with a probability for each label instead of free-form text and are much cheaper and faster. We test this promise on hallucination detection. We build binary benchmarks for five hallucination types (9,852 items from six datasets) and compare five decision models with the generative judge gpt-6-sol. Performance depends strongly on the type: the best decision model matches gpt-6-sol in balanced accuracy on context inconsistency and comes within 3 percentage points on factual errors, but trails it by 4–8 points on logical and instruction inconsistency. Decision-model probabilities are overconfident, though less so than the GPT-6 models, and separate correct from incorrect decisions only moderately. We also find that a confidence cascade of decision models improves on the best single model by 1.9–3.3 points on three types and matches or exceeds gpt-6-sol at 1–3% of its cost. Overall, decision models are a practical low-cost judge for some hallucination types but need to be validated before use.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as judges of model outputs, an approach often called LLM-as-a-Judge Gu et al. (2026); Zheng et al. (2023). They rate open-ended responses Verga et al. (2024); Badshah et al. (2025), check whether responses follow instructions Wen et al. (2026); Zeng et al. (2024), and detect hallucinated content Li et al. (2023); Tang et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2026); Manakul et al. (2023). However, LLM judges are not fully reliable themselves. They can hallucinate, produce incorrect or unsupported judgments, and be overconfident in their judgments Kadavath et al. (2022); Tian et al. (2023).

Recently released decision models offer a different kind of judge. Models such as jev TypeSafe AI (2026), d1 AI (2026), and Perplexity Decider Bespoke Labs and Sathiamoorthy (2026) do not generate free-form assessments but choose among predefined verdicts and return a probability for each. This design has two potential advantages. First, providers present these probabilities as a measure of certainty, so reliable probabilities can show when a judgment should not be trusted TypeSafe AI (2026). Second, decision models are much cheaper and faster than generative LLMs, which matters for large-scale evaluation Li et al. (2026); Rao and Callison-Burch (2026); Ibrahim and Zaki (2026).

Whether these advantages hold is still unclear. Recent studies of decision models as judges each examine a single model Li et al. (2026); Rao and Callison-Burch (2026), leaving several questions open. First, judge performance varies across tasks Xu et al. (2025), but how consistently decision models perform across error types is unknown. Second, whether their probabilities are calibrated and separate correct judgments from errors has merely been tested Xie et al. (2025). Third, multi-judge studies Verga et al. (2024); Ma et al. (2025) have not tested ensembles composed solely of decision models for hallucination detection.

We address these gaps in the context of hallucination detection. First, judge reliability matters most here, since a judge that hallucinates while checking for hallucinations defeats its purpose. Second, hallucination types require different evidence (world knowledge, sources, the response itself, or the prompt), so they test whether decision models can generalize. We ask three research questions:

  • •

    RQ1. How accurately do decision models detect different hallucination types?

  • •

    RQ2. How reliable is their confidence?

  • •

    RQ3. Can ensembles of decision models improve detection accuracy?

We evaluate five decision models against the generative LLM gpt-6-sol on 9,852 samples from six datasets based on five hallucination types Huang et al. (2025). Our results show that decision models can match gpt-6-sol on some hallucination types at a small fraction of its cost, and that most of them are only mildly overconfident. Confidence cascades of decision models further improve the accuracy of hallucination detection. Overall, our results show that decision models are a practical low-cost judge for some hallucination types but should be validated before use.

2 Related Work

LLM-as-a-Judge and Decision Models. LLM-as-a-Judge is widely used for automated evaluation. LLM judges can align with human evaluations (Min et al., 2023) but also show biases such as position and verbosity bias (Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023), and because they generate text, they add cost and latency. In contrast, decision models provide a non-generative alternative by directly selecting from predefined labels and returning their associated probabilities. Recent work evaluates jev on HaluEval factuality and final-answer adjudication (Li et al., 2026), as well as on rubric criteria (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026), and reports lower cost and latency than generative LLM judges. Ibrahim and Zaki (2026) compare several decision models on social-science annotation.

Hallucination detection. Detecting a hallucination requires evidence depending on its type (Huang et al., 2025). FAVABench and HADTest annotate factual errors (Mishra et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026), RAGTruth annotates unsupported or contradictory content in retrieval-grounded responses (Niu et al., 2024), ContraDoc and ROSCOE cover contradictions within documents and reasoning chains (Li et al., 2024; Golovneva et al., 2023), and IF-RewardBench covers instruction following (Wen et al., 2026). AggreFact shows that factuality detector performance varies across datasets, summarizers, and error types (Tang et al., 2023).

Confidence reliability. Returning probabilities does not make a judge’s confidence reliable. Calibration asks whether probabilities match observed frequencies (Guo et al., 2017), and error ranking asks whether confidence separates correct judgments from errors. Language-model confidence can reflect correctness, but this depends on the task and on how confidence is elicited (Kadavath et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024). For decision models, calibration varies by workload (Li et al., 2026; Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026), and high confidence can coexist with near-chance accuracy (Ibrahim and Zaki, 2026).

Judge ensembles and cascades. Combining judges helps when their errors differ. PoLL aggregates judgments from diverse generative models (Verga et al., 2024), and CLEV calls a third judge only when the first two disagree (Badshah et al., 2025), the idea behind our arbitration method. Confidence-based cascades pass uncertain items to another judge (Jung et al., 2025). JEV-to-generative cascades can match the generative judge at lower cost (Li et al., 2026), although overlapping errors limit their gains on rubric tasks (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026).

Three areas remain underexplored. First, decision models have so far been evaluated one at a time or on tasks other than hallucination detection, so it is unclear how well they detect each hallucination type. Second, few studies have examined whether the confidence of decision models is reliable across models and hallucination types. Third, it has not been tested whether ensembles built only from decision models can improve hallucination detection while keeping their cost low. Our study aims to address these research gaps.

3 Data and Methods

3.1 Benchmark Composition

Hallucination types. Hallucination takes several forms. Following the taxonomy of Huang et al. (2025), we study five types (Table 1). Factual contradiction (FC) covers claims that contradict verifiable real-world facts. Factual fabrication (FF) covers unverifiable or unsupported overclaims. Context inconsistency (CI) covers claims that conflict with the supplied source material or are not supported by it. Logical inconsistency (LI) covers contradictions within a response or between its reasoning steps. Instruction inconsistency (II) covers violations of explicit instructions. We treat each type as a separate binary task, because one response can contain several types of error.

Benchmark datasets. We choose six benchmarks whose annotations mark the target error type explicitly, so each sample maps to a binary label without new annotation (Tang et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024). For FC and FF, we combine two datasets that annotate both types, given that FAVABench alone has fewer than 400 samples per type. FAVABench contains ChatGPT and Llama responses with human span-level error annotations (Mishra et al., 2024). HADTest contains responses into which GPT-4o injected a single factual error, validated by two annotators (Xu et al., 2026). For CI, RAGTruth contains responses from six LLMs to question answering, summarization, and data-to-text tasks, annotated for content that conflicts with the retrieved source or is unsupported by it (Niu et al., 2024). For II, IF-RewardBench contains responses from 16 LLMs, each checked against a list of explicit constraints (Wen et al., 2026). For LI, ContraDoc contains news, Wikipedia, and story documents with inserted self-contradictions (Li et al., 2024), and ROSCOE contains step-by-step reasoning annotated for contradictions (Golovneva et al., 2023).

An item is labeled HH if its source annotation marks the target error and NN if it marks the absence of that hallucination error. An NN sample may therefore still contain another type of hallucination. We keep each dataset’s evaluation unit and do not rebalance the classes. Appendix A.3 details how we map each dataset’s original annotations to the binary labels used in our evaluation.

3.2 Evaluation Setup and Metrics

Model selection. We select five decision models from five providers, including both proprietary and open-weight models. They are jev, d1, clef, pplx, and gpt-6-luna. Details of these models are presented in Appendix B. For comparison, we also run the general-purpose generative LLM gpt-6-sol on the same items, distinguishing it from gpt-6-luna, which is included as a decision model because it directly outputs classification decisions. All six models are accessed through their hosted APIs. Latency is therefore end-to-end API response time and does not depend on local hardware.

Model input and output. For each hallucination type, all models receive the same input and the same H/NH/N criterion, based on the type’s definition. The input consists of the response to be judged and, when available, the original instruction. For CI, it also includes the source context. The models never see the gold labels or the annotated error spans. Each model answers HH if the response contains the target error and NN otherwise, and returns probabilities P⁡(H)P(H) and P⁡(N)P(N) that sum to one. The answer is the label with the higher probability, and on an exact tie we keep the model’s own answer. The decision models return these probabilities through their interfaces. For gpt-6-sol, we ask for a structured verdict with its own probability estimates and no explanation. Appendix A.4 provides the complete decision-model prompts.

Evaluation metrics. The classes are imbalanced (Table 1), so we compare each answer with the gold label and report balanced accuracy (BAcc), the mean recall over HH and NN, and macro-F1, the mean F1 over the two classes. Differences between judges are tested with paired bootstrap over items (2,000 resamples) (Dror et al., 2018). We also report the mean API latency per call and the estimated API cost. Cost is computed from recorded token usage at the providers’ list prices at the time of evaluation.22 2 Per million input tokens, $0.042 for jev, $0.04 for d1, $0.24 for clef, $0.02 for pplx, and $0.10 for gpt-6-luna. The decision models return a single choice token, so their output cost is negligible. For gpt-6-sol, $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

3.3 Confidence Analysis

Probabilities and confidence. For each item ii, a decision model returns pi=P⁡(H∣xi)p_{i}=P(\textsc{H}\mid x_{i}), the probability that the response contains the target hallucination type, and labels the response as hallucinated (y^i=1\hat{y}_{i}=1) when pi>0.5p_{i}>0.5. Providers describe pip_{i} as an estimate of the probability that the predicate holds or as a calibrated score. The confidence of a decision is the probability of its predicted label,

ci=max⁡(pi, 1−pi)∈[0.5,1].c_{i}=\max(p_{i},\,1-p_{i})\in[0.5,1]. (1)

Under perfect calibration, predictions assigned confidence qq would be correct approximately qq of the time. We evaluate the extent to which this property holds in practice.

Detection and calibration. Detection performance, i.e., how well pip_{i} ranks hallucinated above non-hallucinated responses, is measured by AUROC. At τ=0.5\tau=0.5, we also report BAcc, MCC and the flag-rate bias Δ\Delta (defined as the share of responses flagged minus π\pi (Δ>0\Delta>0: over-flagging). Calibration is measured by the expected calibration error over M=10M=10 equal-width confidence bins (Guo et al., 2017; Roelofs et al., 2022):

ECE=∑m=1M|Bm|n​|acc⁡(Bm)−conf⁡(Bm)|.\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\tfrac{|B_{m}|}{n}\,\bigl|\mathrm{acc}(B_{m})-\mathrm{conf}(B_{m})\bigr|. (2)

where BmB_{m} is the set of predictions in confidence bin mm. We also report the slope bb of the logistic model logit⁡Pr⁡(yi=1)=a+b​logit⁡(pi)\operatorname{logit}\Pr(y_{i}{=}1)=a+b\operatorname{logit}(p_{i}), where b<1b<1 indicates overconfidence (Calster, 2019).

Confidence as an error signal. A useful confidence score is expected to be higher for correct decisions (𝒞\mathcal{C}) than for errors (ℰ\mathcal{E}) (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017):

conf-AUROC=Pr⁡(ci>cj∣i∈𝒞,j∈ℰ),\text{conf-AUROC}=\Pr(c_{i}>c_{j}\mid i\in\mathcal{C},\,j\in\mathcal{E}), (3)

with ties counted as one half. A value of 0.50.5 means that confidence cannot distinguish correct decisions from errors. We also report the share of errors made with high confidence (ci≥0.9c_{i}\geq 0.9).

We report 95% bootstrap intervals and compare models on the same items with paired bootstrap tests. A two-way ANOVA (η2\eta^{2}) separates cell and model effects, and Kendall’s WW measures ranking consistency across cells.

3.4 Model Ensembling Strategies

Motivated by prior studies Verga et al. (2024); Badshah et al. (2025); Jung et al. (2025), we evaluate three ensembling methods (Figure 1) to assess whether they improve accuracy and at what additional cost. To isolate the effect of each method, we fix the model selection. For each type, all three methods combine the same three decision models, namely those with the highest BAcc on that type.

Majority voting. All three models judge the same item, and the label chosen by at least two of them is the verdict. Because every item gets all three calls, majority voting is the most expensive of the three methods. Voting gives every model the same weight, so two weaker models can outvote the strongest one.

Arbitration. When two models agree, the outcome is their shared label, and the third vote does not change it. When they disagree, the third vote decides the outcome. Arbitration therefore calls the two models first and calls the third only to resolve a disagreement (Badshah et al., 2025).

Confidence cascade. A cascade lets the strongest model decide unless it is uncertain. Cascades usually order models from cheap to expensive to reduce calls to a costly final model (Chen et al., 2024; Jung et al., 2025). We order the models by descending BAcc and ask whether consulting weaker models on the strongest model’s least confident items improves BAcc (Jitkrittum et al., 2023). At each of the first two stages, a model defers an item to the next model when its confidence cic_{i} falls below a threshold, and the third model decides all items that reach it. Because confidence distributions differ across models (Section 4.2), a common threshold would defer very different shares of items at different stages. We therefore set each threshold through a target deferral rate rkr_{k}, the share of items reaching stage kk that are deferred, so that each stage defers its least confident items without using gold labels. We evaluate r1,r2∈{0,0.1,…,0.5}r_{1},r_{2}\in\{0,0.1,\ldots,0.5\}: r1=0r_{1}=0 reduces the cascade to the strongest model, and above 0.50.5 the strongest model would decide fewer than half of the items. As a control, we defer the same numbers of randomly chosen items.

Evaluation. For each hallucination type, we evaluate all 6×66\times 6 combinations of r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} and report the one with the highest BAcc. Because we choose this combination on the same items we evaluate, the result is an optimistic estimate of what a cascade can achieve(Cawley and Talbot, 2010). To see how optimistic it is, we also choose the rates with five-fold cross-fitting, picking them on four folds and testing them on the fifth. The cost of an item is the total cost of all models called for it. For latency, we add up calls made one after another and take the slowest of calls made in parallel. We plot each method’s BAcc against its cost, show the results of all 36 combinations separately, and use paired bootstrap tests to compare each method with its best single model and with gpt-6-sol.

4 Results

4.1 RQ1: How Do Decision Models Perform Across Hallucination Types?

Table 2 and Figure 2 present the performance over each hallucination type. Appendix C reports their performance judge on every source dataset.

Performance depends strongly on the type. gpt-6-sol has the highest pooled BAcc on FC, LI, and II (Table 2). On FF, gpt-6-luna (82.7) edges it (82.0). On CI, pplx, gpt-6-sol, and jev are within 0.2 points of one another at about 82.6. The gap is widest on II, where gpt-6-sol reaches 78.9 against 71.1 for pplx and 61.8 for jev. Performance also varies within a model. jev spans 20.8 points between II and CI. Type and source dataset are confounded, so we read these differences as type-specific without attributing them to the type alone.

Similar scores hide different errors. The matched CI scores arise from different error patterns. pplx rarely raises false alarms (false-positive rate 3.2%) but misses many hallucinations (false-negative rate 31.5%). gpt-6-sol shows the reverse pattern, with a false-negative rate of 5.9% and a false-positive rate of 28.8%. jev lies between them at 20.6% and 14.4%. The dominant error also changes with the task. jev misses most positives on LI, with false-negative rates of 49% on ContraDoc and 81% on ROSCOE, but over-flags on II, where its false-positive rate is 56%. BAcc alone therefore does not show whether a judge mostly misses hallucinations or mostly raises false alarms.

Model advantages are concentrated in particular types. Relative to jev, pplx gains only 0.1 points on CI (95% paired bootstrap interval [−1.4,1.6][-1.4,1.6]) and loses 0.9 points on FF ([−3.4,1.6][-3.4,1.6]), but it gains 3.9 points on FC ([1.5,6.4][1.5,6.4]), 4.3 points on LI ([2.2,6.5][2.2,6.5]), and 9.3 points on II ([7.2,11.5][7.2,11.5]). The FC, LI, and II gains remain significant after Holm correction over the 25 comparisons of each judge with jev. The ranking of decision models thus changes with the type.

Advantages do not always hold across sources. On HADTest, all six judges score 12 to 18 points higher on FF than on FC. The same comparison on FAVABench shows no consistent gap (Appendix C). For pplx, FF minus FC is −1.4-1.4 points on FAVABench (95% bootstrap interval [−8.5,5.3][-8.5,5.3]) but 17.917.9 points on HADTest ([13.2,22.9][13.2,22.9]). An advantage on fabrication is therefore partly a property of the source. CI and II each have a single source, so their cross-source stability remains untested.

Decision models are far cheaper and faster. Per item, the decision models cost between 0.5% (pplx) and 10% (clef) of gpt-6-sol, and they answer in 0.22 to 0.62 seconds against 1.6 to 2.6 seconds (Table 2). The cheapest model, pplx, is also the most accurate decision model on four of the five types, and gpt-6-luna is the most accurate on FF. The efficiency gain is thus available on every type. Whether it comes with the accuracy of gpt-6-sol depends on the type. Additional analyses of error patterns and prediction overlap across models are provided in Appendix D.2.

4.2 RQ2: How Reliable is Their Confidence?

Figures 3 and 4 present the confidence reliability of the six judges across hallucination types, including calibration and the ability to distinguish correct judgments from errors.

Decision models are overconfident overall, but less so than the GPT-6 models. Every decision model has a positive average overconfidence gap, and the calibration slope is below 1 for 21 of the 25 model–type pairs (Figure 3a). For jev, pplx, clef and d1, however, the overconfidence is mild. Mean confidence exceeds accuracy by 0.040.04–0.120.12, and ECE ranges from 0.0830.083 to 0.1360.136. The two GPT-6 models are clearly more overconfident. gpt-6-luna has a gap of 0.180.18 and an ECE of 0.1870.187, and the comparison LLM gpt-6-sol has a gap of 0.160.16 and an ECE of 0.1570.157. Their median calibration slopes (0.440.44 and 0.360.36) are also the lowest, compared with 0.540.54–0.580.58 for jev, d1 and pplx and 0.960.96 for clef.

Calibration depends more on the dataset than on the model. Across the decision models, the dataset accounts for 58% of the variance in the overconfidence gap, and the model for 15% (Figure 3a). Averaged over the decision models, overconfidence is largest for II (0.140.14) and LI (0.130.13), and smallest for CI and factual contradiction FC (0.070.07 each). The reliability diagrams show the same pattern. At a given confidence level, accuracy differs by hallucination type (Figure 4). For example, the accuracy of gpt-6-luna on CI stays below 0.500.50 for all confidence levels between 0.550.55 and 0.950.95.

Confidence is less reliable for instruction inconsistency (II) and logical inconsistency (LI). Averaged over the decision models, II has the largest overconfidence gap (0.140.14), the highest ECE (0.1450.145) and the lowest conf-AUROC (0.640.64), followed by LI (gap 0.130.13; ECE 0.1360.136; conf-AUROC 0.700.70). FC is less overconfident (gap 0.070.07; ECE 0.1030.103) but separates correct from incorrect decisions no better than LI (conf-AUROC 0.700.70), whereas CI (gap 0.070.07; ECE 0.0930.093; conf-AUROC 0.740.74) and FF(gap 0.080.08; ECE 0.1340.134; conf-AUROC 0.750.75) are the most reliable. Figure 3 shows the same pattern. Among decisions made with c≥0.9c\geq 0.9, accuracy is lowest for II for jev and pplx, and for LI for clef and d1 (Figure 4). Type-specific failures also occur for individual models. gpt-6-luna is most overconfident on CI (gap 0.310.31), where its accuracy stays below 0.500.50.

Confidence separates correct from incorrect decisions only moderately. conf-AUROC measures how well confidence separates correct judgments from errors. A value of 0.50.5 indicates performance no better than chance. Higher values indicate better separation between the two groups (Figure 3b). Averaged over the five hallucination types, conf-AUROC ranges from 0.670.67 (gpt-6-luna) to 0.730.73 (pplx and clef). For each model and type, the 95% confidence interval lies above 0.50.5, so confidence always carries some information about correctness, but the separation remains moderate, especially for II.

High confidence does not guarantee a correct decision. Errors can be made with high confidence (c≥0.9c\geq 0.9) (Figures 4 and 7). Averaged over the five types, gpt-6-luna assigns c≥0.9c\geq 0.9 to 65% of its decisions, is correct on only 77% of them, and makes 47% of its errors at this level. For the other decision models, 10–30% of errors are made at c≥0.9c\geq 0.9, with clef lowest (10%); clef also assigns such high confidence to only 25% of its decisions. The comparison model gpt-6-sol is the most extreme case: it assigns c≥0.9c\geq 0.9 to 88% of its decisions and makes 69% of its errors at this level.

4.3 RQ3: Can Ensembling Improve the Performance?

Figure 5 presents the performance–cost trade-offs of the three ensembling methods. Deferral-rate sensitivity is reported in Appendix Figure 8.

The cascade matches or exceeds GPT-6-sol on three types. At the best tested deferral rates, the confidence cascade achieves BAcc scores of 82.2, 84.6, and 84.6 on FC, FF, and CI, respectively—0.6, 2.6, and 1.9 points higher than gpt-6-sol—at only 1.2–3.3% of its estimated cost. The advantage over gpt-6-sol is statistically significant on FF and CI, but not on FC. The cascade also improves on the strongest single member by 3.3, 1.9, and 2.0 points, respectively, with paired bootstrap 95% intervals excluding zero. It makes 1.1–1.3 calls per item and has about one fifth of the latency of gpt-6-sol. Selecting deferral rates by cross-fitting reduces BAcc by at most 0.52 points and preserves the gains over the strongest member.

The cascade outperforms voting and arbitration. Majority voting gains about one BAcc point over the strongest single model on FC and FF, but falls below it on CI, LI, and II (Figure 5). Disagreement arbitration produces the same verdicts as voting while costing roughly half as much. Both rules are less accurate than the cascade on every type and, except on FF, also cost more. Unlike equal voting, the cascade consults weaker members only when the strongest member is uncertain.

The best cascade configuration differs by type. pplx leads four of the five cascades. On FF, gpt-6-luna leads (Appendix Table 12). The role of the later stages also varies. On CI, the best cascade never uses its third model (r2=0r_{2}=0), whereas on FF the second model defers about half of the samples it receives. On FC, FF, and CI, BAcc peaks at a first-stage deferral rate of 20–30% and declines at higher rates (Appendix Figure 8). A single cascade configuration therefore does not transfer across types.

The gap persists on LI and II. On LI, the best cascade defers no items and equals pplx alone, 3.9 points below gpt-6-sol. On II, the cascade improves BAcc by only 0.7 points over the strongest single model, pplx, and remains 7.1 points below gpt-6-sol. Other members do not improve on pplx for its least confident items in balanced terms, consistent with the weaker confidence reliability on these two types (Section 4.2).

5 Discussion and Conclusion

We evaluate five decision models for hallucination detection. They match or approach the generative LLM judge on factual and context-related errors but lag on logical and instruction inconsistencies requiring multi-step reasoning or explicit constraint checking. We draw three takeaways.

First, judges should be selected per hallucination type. No decision model performs best across types, and similar BAcc can mask opposite error profiles: missed hallucinations or false alarms. The preferable judge thus depends on the target type and on which error is more costly, so false-negative and false-positive rates should be reported by type. Since type and source are partly confounded, judge selection should be validated on the target task.

Second, confidence is useful but does not guarantee correctness. Most decision models are less overconfident than gpt-6-luna and gpt-6-sol, but their confidence only moderately distinguishes correct from incorrect judgments, with frequent high-confidence errors on logical and instruction inconsistencies (Section 4.2). Confidence can guide requests for a second opinion but cannot establish correctness.

Third, ensembling decision models helps when they are complementary on uncertain samples. Cascades outperform their strongest member and match or exceed gpt-6-sol on factual contradiction, factual fabrication, and context inconsistency. On logical and instruction inconsistency, the tested cascades offer limited gains, consistent with the observed error overlap (Appendix D.2). Since the best configuration varies by type, deferral rates should be validated on the target type to weigh accuracy gains against the cost of additional model calls.

At 0.5–10% of the cost of gpt-6-sol, decision models could support low-cost, type-aware cascades for factual and context errors, with LLM judges reserved for logical and instruction inconsistencies. Future work should disentangle type from data source, develop decision models that target reasoning- and instruction-level errors, and learn routing policies that decide when to escalate to an LLM judge based on detection accuracy and cost.

Limitations

This study presents several future directions.

Benchmark coverage and label consistency. Our benchmark covers five hallucination types across six datasets, but coverage is uneven: context and instruction inconsistency each rely on a single source. Differences in data construction, domain, and response length confound cross-dataset comparisons, leaving subgroup analyses observational. Mapping heterogeneous annotations to binary labels may also introduce mismatches because the source datasets define errors differently. Broader source coverage, annotation under a shared rubric, and comparisons matched on domain and response length would help address these limitations.

Confidence comparability and prompt sensitivity. Confidence values are not fully comparable because decision models return label probabilities, whereas gpt-6-sol reports its own estimates. We also use one prompt design per task, leaving prompt sensitivity untested. Comparing alternative prompts and, where supported, confidence-elicitation methods within each model would clarify their effects on accuracy and calibration.

Generalization and deployment of cascades. We evaluate fixed model versions and assess cascades through offline replay and within-source cross-fitting, with member selection and ordering based on the full sample. Selecting all cascade components using training data alone, followed by evaluation on unseen domains and in live deployments, would better assess their accuracy, latency, and cost beyond the evaluated settings.

Statement of LLM Use

During the preparation of this paper, we used LLM-based tools (primarily Claude and ChatGPT) in two capacities. First, we used coding agents to assist with the development and refinement of the project codebase. Second, we used LLM chatbots to support language editing of manuscript drafts, including correcting grammatical errors, improving sentence structure, and enhancing the clarity of presentation. The authors take full responsibility for the content of this paper, including the code, analyses, and conclusions presented.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Benchmark Construction, Labels, and Prompts

A.1 Hallucination Taxonomy and Examples

Type and definition Example dialog Annotation
Factuality hallucination
Factual Contradiction States facts that can be grounded in real-world knowledge but contradict it, through a wrong entity or relation. Instruction: How does the EU work? Response: The EU also has its own currency, the euro, which is used by 19 member states. FAVABench, entity error; the correct number is 20.
Factual Fabrication States facts that cannot be verified against established knowledge, or overclaims without broad support. Instruction: Name three important inventions of the 20th century. Response: The three important inventions of the 20th century are the airplane, the automobile, and the chromoflare device, which enabled seamless digital color transitions in electronic displays. HADTest, fabricated entity; no such device exists.
Faithfulness hallucination
Context Inconsistency Is unfaithful to the context supplied by the user, such as a retrieved document. Retrieved context: Three of the alleged attackers were killed, Israeli media reported, citing IDF sources. It was not immediately known to what militant group the men belonged. Instruction: Summarize the following news within 38 words. Response: Israeli jets struck targets in the occupied Golan Heights after militants attempted to plant a bomb near the Israeli border. Four alleged attackers were killed, but their affiliation remains unclear. RAGTruth, evident conflict; the source reports three deaths.
Logical Inconsistency Contains internal contradictions, between statements or reasoning steps, or between the steps and the conclusion. Document: The text of this novel of ideas presents itself as a book that has been written as the result of a promise to a dying man. William Porphyry Benham is a man who has lived a life devoted to a complicated, protean idea: “that he had to live life nobly and thoroughly.” The novel has been written as the result of a bet between two friends. ContraDoc; the last sentence contradicts the first.
Instruction Inconsistency Deviates from an explicit, non-malicious user instruction. Instruction: what concentration of particles is bad for biosensors. The output should not contain any whitespace. Response: Particle concentrations exceeding 1mg/mL or 107particles/mL often cause biosensor interference depending on sensor type particle size and matrix. IF-RewardBench; whitespace violates the instruction.

Table 3 lists the five hallucination types, their definitions, and benchmark examples.

A.2 Dataset Versions and Construction

Table 4 identifies the source snapshots, evaluation subsets, and resulting type-specific views. Revisions refer to the local source snapshots used to build the benchmark. Where an upstream revision was not retained, a SHA-256 fingerprint identifies the archived source file. Hashes below use the first 12 hexadecimal characters; the accompanying provenance file records the complete hashes and revision identifiers for the archived source snapshots.

Factuality mapping and reuse.

For FAVABench, entity, relation, and contradictory map to FC; invented, unverifiable, and subjective map to FF, with subjective treated as overclaim. We reconstruct the annotated error-bearing passage by removing proposed corrections inside mark spans and stripping annotation tags while retaining their content, including delete spans. A response carrying both types is positive in both views. Negatives have none of the six factual error tags; responses carrying only the other type are excluded. Thus, 115 jointly positive and 153 jointly negative records are reused across FC and FF.

For HADTest, Factual Recall Error and Factual Inference Error map to FC, while Fabricated Entity and Fictional Attribution map to FF. The 1,124 None-labeled responses are negatives in both views; other categories are excluded. The conversion removes empty responses and conflicting-label duplicate texts, retaining the first occurrence of a same-label duplicate within a view. Reuse across types is intentional because the two tasks ask different questions of the same response.

Faithfulness subsets.

RAGTruth is positive when at least one hallucination span is annotated, after the test/good filtering. ContraDoc includes both inserted and replacement-based contradictions. ROSCOE uses the whole-chain 0_full_newClearContradiction_result label (yes/no); this annotation also mentions incoherent reasoning, so the view is broader than strict contradiction. Its 756 released rows yield 755 evaluable chains after excluding one empty CosmosQA response. IF-RewardBench’s English filter retains instructions and checklists containing no characters in U+4E00--U+9FFF; it is a preprocessing heuristic, not a separate official language split. The retained responses comprise 984 single-turn, 574 multi-turn, and 736 system-prompt items. Any violated constraint maps to HH.

Counting convention.

The total of 9,852 counts type-specific evaluation instances, not deduplicated answers. The 268 shared FAVABench records and 1,124 shared HADTest records account for the cross-type reuse. There are 8,460 distinct (dataset, source-record ID) pairs; this is an ID count, not global text deduplication. Judges receive complete responses, documents, or reasoning chains, without gold labels, annotated spans, or corrections.

A.3 Binary Label Mapping

Figure 6 shows how we map each dataset’s original annotations to binary labels. For each hallucination type, an item is labeled HH if its annotations indicate the target error and NN if they indicate its absence. FAVABench and HADTest provide annotations for both factual types, so we construct separate FC and FF views from each. In FAVABench, a response is negative only if it carries none of the six factual error tags. Responses tagged only with the other factual type are excluded. In HADTest, None-labeled responses serve as negatives for both FC and FF, and we exclude its other error categories. RAGTruth labels a response as HH if it contains at least one annotated hallucination span. ContraDoc uses its official split, and ROSCOE uses its whole-chain ClearContradiction label. In IF-RewardBench, a response is labeled HH if it violates any annotated constraint. We keep each dataset’s original evaluation unit. Because some annotations target a single error type, NN means only that the target error is absent, not that the output is error-free.

A.4 Decision-Model Prompts

Decision models have no separate system and user prompts. Each request carries a choice question, which is fixed for a hallucination type, and an item state, which is filled for each record. The decision models (jev, d1, clef, and pplx) receive both parts; gpt-6-luna receives the same text through the OpenAI Decisions API, with the state serialized as a JSON string and the HH/NN criteria given as choice descriptions. Bracketed values are placeholders for the item text. A state field is sent only when it is non-empty. The shared request structure is shown below. The type-specific instructions and criteria are reproduced verbatim below; field headings are added for display, and the state fields retain the original placeholders.

Appendix D Error Analysis

D.1 Errors by Source Annotation

Table 9 breaks recall of HH down by attributes available in the source annotations. The attributes are the number of annotated error spans or violated constraints, the salience of the error, the task form, and the model that generated the judged response. Where both classes are present, the table reports BAcc instead of recall.

D.2 Error Patterns and Overlap

Errors concentrate on sparse and subtle targets.

To locate where decision models fail, we break recall of HH down by the source annotations (Table 9). The amount of evidence matters most. On RAGTruth, pplx recovers 57% of responses with one annotated span but 96% of those with three or more. On IF-RewardBench, it recovers 46% of responses that violate one constraint but 74% of those that violate three or more. gpt-6-sol recovers 91% and 76% of the single-error cases. Salience matters next. The recall of pplx drops from 71% to 42% for RAGTruth spans annotated only as subtle, and from 91% to 32% for ContraDoc contradictions created by replacing a sentence rather than inserting one. Task form matters as well. All decision models fall to 47 to 63% BAcc on multi-turn instructions, and every judge, including gpt-6-sol, is close to chance on the non-arithmetic ROSCOE chains. The generative judge is not uniformly better either. On RAGTruth data-to-text items, pplx reaches 86% BAcc against 79% for gpt-6-sol.

Decision-model errors overlap only partly with the generative judge.

pplx and gpt-6-sol are both wrong on 4% of CI items, 6 to 8% of FC and FF items, and 11 to 13% of LI and II items. The Jaccard overlap of their error sets rises from 0.13 on CI to 0.50 on LI. Overlap among decision models is higher and is again largest on LI, between 0.51 and 0.57 for pplx against each other decision model. Errors are thus least shared on the types where decision models are already strong and most shared where they are weak. This pattern anticipates RQ3.

Appendix E Confidence Analysis Details

Confidence and hallucination type.

To test whether the accuracy implied by a confidence level depends on the hallucination type tt, we fit, for each decision model, logit⁡Pr⁡(y^i=yi)=β0+β1​ci+γt+δt​ci\operatorname{logit}\Pr(\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i})=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}c_{i}+\gamma_{t}+\delta_{t}c_{i}, with standard errors clustered by response, and test δt=0\delta_{t}=0 for all tt. The interaction is significant for every model (Wald χ2=57\chi^{2}=57–142142, all p<10−10p<10^{-10}).

Confidence distributions.

Figure 7 shows, for each model, how its correct decisions and its errors are distributed over confidence. For a useful confidence score, errors should concentrate at low confidence and correct decisions at high confidence. This holds most clearly for clef, whose errors are spread over the lower confidence range and only 10% of which fall at c≥0.9c\geq 0.9. For gpt-6-luna and especially gpt-6-sol, the error distribution peaks in the highest confidence bin, much like that of correct decisions, so high confidence alone does not reliably distinguish between the two.

Robustness check of the calibration results.

The ECE ranking of the models is unchanged under 15 equal-width bins, under 10 or 15 equal-mass bins, and under a debiased ECE. Clipping probabilities at 10−210^{-2} instead of 10−410^{-4} changes each model’s median calibration slope by at most 0.090.09.

Appendix F Cascade Deferral-Rate Sensitivity

Figure 8 shows sensitivity to two target deferral rates: r1r_{1} is the fraction of all items passed from the first member to the second, and r2r_{2} is the fraction of second-stage items passed to the third. Each stage defers its least-confident items. At r1=0r_{1}=0, all curves coincide with the strongest member alone.

Moderate deferral helps selected types.

FC, FF, and CI peak at intermediate r1r_{1} values (20–30%), reaching 82.2%, 84.6%, and 84.6% BAcc, respectively; larger rates eventually reduce performance. The separation between curves also shows sensitivity to r2r_{2}, particularly for FC and CI. LI performs best without deferral: every tested nonzero r1r_{1} lowers BAcc. II gains at most 0.7 percentage points over the strongest member and remains 7.1 points below gpt-6-sol. Thus, deferring more low-confidence items does not consistently improve accuracy; the benefit depends on the hallucination type and both operating rates.

F.1 Peak and Cross-Fitted Results

Peak settings maximize pooled BAcc on the 36-point grid. Cross-fitting uses five label-stratified folds and seeds 0–4: fit rates and confidence thresholds on four folds, then apply them to the held-out fold. Members stay ordered by full-sample BAcc, so this checks rate/threshold selection, not the full model-selection pipeline. Ties use ascending (r1,r2)(r_{1},r_{2}) order.

Cross-fitting lowers BAcc by at most 0.52 points. FC, FF, and CI retain gains over the strongest member, with intervals excluding zero. Their cross-fitted differences from gpt-6-sol have intervals containing zero. LI always selects no deferral; II has no clear gain over its strongest member.
